entry.title: Fred-Tutavaha v Assistant Minister for Citizenship, Customs and Multicultural Affairs [2026] FCA 1586
entry.content:
The applicant, a New Zealand citizen who arrived in Australia aged four, sought judicial review of the Assistant Minister's decision under s 501BA of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to set aside an AAT decision revoking the cancellation of his visa. He ran three grounds — unreasonable delay, failure to consider immigration detention as a legal consequence, and legal unreasonableness in giving legal consequences "neutral weight" — with the Court also considering a proposed fourth ground on the national interest assessment.

Key holding: A failure to refer expressly to immigration detention in reasons for a s 501BA cancellation does not permit an inference that this legal consequence was not considered, where detention pending removal is an obvious and well-known statutory consequence and there is no barrier to removal.

It does not follow, however, that the proper inference is that the Assistant Minister failed to appreciate that a legal consequence of his decision was that the Applicant would be taken into immigration detention. The statement of reasons must be read fairly and as a whole, and the fact that a matter is not mentioned expressly does not necessarily mean it was not considered

entry.title: "Automotive, Food, Metals, Engineering, Printing and Kindred Industries Union" known as the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) (188V) v Schindler Lifts Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4166
entry.content:
The AMWU referred a dispute under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) and clause 10 of the Schindler Lifts Australia Pty Ltd Victorian Enterprise Agreement 2024–2028, asking how the "make up pay for workers comp" entitlement in clause 42 is calculated. The Commission held that "average weekly earnings" in clause 42 is to be worked out by reference to the Victorian workers' compensation concept of pre-injury average weekly earnings under the WIRC Act, and left the arithmetic to the parties.

Key holding: Where an enterprise agreement requires a top-up to 100% of "average weekly earnings" but does not define the term, that expression is to be calculated by reference to the pre-injury average weekly earnings concept in the Victorian workers' compensation legislation, with either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act available.

As such, I consider that Mr Savari's 'average weekly earnings' for the purposes of clause 42 of the 2024 Agreement in relation to his workers' compensation claim for injury for the injury on 20 March 2025 are able to be calculated by reference to either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act.

entry.title: Application by The Australian Maritime Officers' Union (001N) & The Australian Institute of Marine and Power Engineers (009V) [2026] FWC 4170
entry.content:
The AMOU and AIMPE sought a regulated labour hire arrangement order under s 306E of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), naming Cyan Vessel as regulated host and One Ocean as employer for crew on the Offshore Solution. The Commission found One Ocean supplied the crew to Cyan Subsea, not Cyan Vessel, and that Cyan Vessel was not the regulated host and its enterprise agreements were not covered employment instruments. The application was dismissed.

Key holding: An application under s 306E fails where the purported regulated host is not the entity to whom the labour hire employees are supplied to perform work and the enterprise agreements relied on are not covered employment instruments for that host.

For the following reasons, I have concluded that Cyan Vessel is not the regulated host and that the Cyan Vessel EAs are not covered employment inst ruments as contemplated by s 306E(1)(b) of the Act.

entry.title: Elizabeth O'Donnell v Fresleven Pty Ltd ATF The Muley Graves Unit Trust T/As Coral Bay Ecotours & Roger Bailye and Others [2026] FWC 4171
entry.content:
Ms O’Donnell brought a s.365 general protections application against Fresleven Pty Ltd and others, alleging she had been dismissed. The Commission determined a jurisdictional objection that she had not been dismissed. Deputy President O’Keeffe found no dismissal was communicated, upheld the objection and dismissed the application.

Key holding: A termination of employment is not effective unless the employer communicates it to the employee in clear and unequivocal terms; allusion or insinuation is insufficient.

As I read them the proposition is that an employee is not terminated until they are advised in clear and unequivocal terms that they are terminated. It is not sufficient to allude or insinuate - the employee must be told.

entry.title: Application by Cv Infrastructure Services Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4172
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission approved the CV Infrastructure Services Enterprise Agreement 2026, a single-enterprise agreement in the electrical contracting industry, subject to written undertakings. The Commission excused a minor NERR naming discrepancy under s 188(5) and found the agreement passed the Better Off Overall Test after clarifications about apprentices and allowances.

Key holding: A minor procedural or technical error in an NERR under s 174(1A) may be excused under s 188(5) where the agreement would otherwise have been genuinely agreed and employees were not likely to be disadvantaged.

However, I am satisfied that the Agreement would have been genuinely agreed to but for th e minor procedural departure from the prescribed form requirements of the NERR under s.174(1A) of the Act and that the employees covered by the Agreement were not likely to have been disadvantaged by this. Accordingly, I exercise the discretion conferred by s.188(5) of the Act.

entry.title: Mr Brandan Bowman-Clift v Unmatched Support Services Pty Ltd & Mr Tuneer Swami [2026] FWC 4152
entry.content:
Mr Bowman-Clift applied under s 365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), alleging dismissal in contravention of Part 3-1. His application was 22 days late, and he sought an extension based on alleged stalling/manipulation by the employer’s founder. The Fair Work Commission refused an extension and dismissed the application.

Key holding: The Commission may extend time under s 366(1)(b) only where satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist after considering the s 366(2) factors.

The Commission can extend time only if it is satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances. Taking into account all matters including those in s.366(2) of the Act, I am not satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances in this case.

entry.content:

entry.title: Application by Queensland Police Citizens Youth Welfare Association [2026] FWC 4157
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined an employer’s application under s.120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to reduce Ms Ashleigh Silver’s redundancy pay to nil after it offered her redeployment to another OSHC Educator role. Ms Silver declined the role because of care arrangements for her puppy and did not file any submissions opposing the application. The Commission found the alternative employment acceptable and reduced the redundancy entitlement to nil.

Key holding: Under s.120, the Commission may reduce redundancy pay to nil where the employer has obtained objectively acceptable alternative employment, notwithstanding the employee’s personal reasons for refusing it.

I am satisfied that that the redeployment role is acceptable alternative employment. The role has the same rate of pay, the same classification level, and the same hours.

entry.title: Application by Raquel Gray [2026] FWC 4143
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined an unfair termination remedy application by a regulated road transport contractor, Ms Gray, against BESB Couriers after she was replaced on the Toukley delivery run upon returning from leave. The Commission found there was no valid reason for termination and that the Road Transport Industry Termination Code processes were not followed, so the termination was unfair. It ordered that a new services contract be entered into between BESB Couriers and Ms Gray personally.

Key holding: A regulated road transport contractor’s termination is unfair where there is no valid reason for termination and the processes under the Road Transport Industry Termination Code are not followed.

In summary, there was no valid reason for the termination of the services contract, and the processes in the Road Transport Code were not followed, in part because of a breakdown in communication and in part because BESB Couriers is a small business with l imited access to resources or relevant legal or human resources expertise. I am satisfied that the termination of the services contract was unfair.

entry.title: Mr Marco Maletti v Kitcraft Kitchens Pty Ltd Trading AS Kitchen Craftsmen [2026] FWC 4162
entry.content:
Marco Maletti applied under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for unfair dismissal after resigning from Kitcraft Kitchens Pty Ltd on 29 January 2026. The employer objected that the Fair Work Commission lacked jurisdiction because Mr Maletti was not dismissed. The FWC upheld the jurisdictional objection and dismissed the application.

Key holding: An employee relying on acceptance of repudiation to establish dismissal must elect to treat the repudiation as ending the contract and must not have affirmed it by continuing the employment.

Secondly, that the Applicant had elected to treat the repudiation as bringing the contract to an end. Thirdly and finally, that the Applicant had not affirmed the contract and continued it.

entry.title: Mr Peter Deane v Hawkesbury Pools Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4093
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dismissed Mr Deane’s unfair dismissal application against Hawkesbury Pools Pty Ltd ([2026] FWC 4093). The employer established it was a small business and that the summary dismissal for establishing and advertising a competing business was consistent with the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code. Because Code consistency meant the dismissal could not be unfair, the Commission did not determine the merits.

Key holding: For a summary dismissal under the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, the Commission determines whether the employer held a belief that the employee’s conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal and whether that belief was based on reasonable grounds, not whether the dismissal was valid or warranted.

First, there needs to be a consideration whether, at the time of dismissal, the employer held a belief that the employee's conduct was sufficiently serious to justify immediate dismissal. Secondly it is necessary to consider whether that belief was based on reasonable grounds.

entry.title: Rasier Pacific Pty Ltd v Ali Hamza [2026] FWC 4164
entry.content:
Uber sought a stay under s 606 of the Fair Work Act 2009 of a Fair Work Commission order requiring it to reactivate Mr Ali Hamza’s access to its digital platform pending appeal. At first instance the Commissioner found moderate speeding was not a valid reason for deactivation and that Uber had not complied with the Digital Labour Platform Deactivation Code. Deputy President Easton refused the stay, finding no reasonable prospects on the merits and no balance of convenience favouring it.

Key holding: A stay under s 606 requires an arguable case with reasonable prospects on both permission to appeal and the substantive merits, together with a balance of convenience favouring the stay.

In determining whether to grant a stay application the Commission must be satisfied that there is an arguable case, with some reasonable prospect of success, in respect of both the question of leave to appeal and the substantive merits of the appeal. In addition, the balance of convenience must weigh in favour of the order subject to appeal being stayed.

entry.title: Daniel Cowell v Brief Access Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4165
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dealt with an unfair dismissal application by Daniel Cowell against Brief Access Pty Ltd (the named respondent; the extract also refers to Brief Labour Co Pty Ltd). The Commission rejected the employer’s jurisdictional objection that it was a small business entitled to rely on the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, found the dismissal unfair, declined reinstatement and ordered compensation. The extract does not reproduce the final compensation calculation or full orders.

Key holding: To rely on summary dismissal under the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, an employer’s belief that conduct is sufficiently serious must be based on reasonable grounds, ordinarily including discussion with the employee and regard to their explanation.

Normally in order to hold a belief on reasonable grounds it will be necessary to have a discussion with the employee about the perceived serious misconduct and pay regard to the explanations and views given by the employee.

entry.title: Secretary, Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure v Thaler (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 226
entry.content:
The NSW Court of Appeal dealt with a notice of motion by the Secretary seeking variations to earlier orders remitting disciplinary proceedings and costs to NCAT. The Court refused to vary the remitter because its scope was already clear, but directed NCAT under cl 29(8)(d) that it may determine the remitted costs of the appeal without being satisfied of special circumstances. It otherwise dismissed the motion, with no order as to the costs of the motion.

Key holding: The Court of Appeal may, under cl 29(8)(d) of Sch 5 to the NCAT Act, direct NCAT to determine remitted costs without requiring special circumstances under s 60.

The power extends to authorising the Tribunal to depart from the rule in s 60 (which rule is explicitly displaced in a number of places in the Act: see Schedule 3 cll 12 and 13 and Schedule 5 cll 23 and 26, and Civil and Administrative Tribunal Rules 2014, rr 38 and 38A).

entry.title: Mr John Tzaferis v Vendro Construction Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4150
entry.content:
Mr John Tzaferis lodged a general protections dismissal application one day late and sought an extension of time under s 366 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Fair Work Commission found exceptional circumstances based principally on representative error by the applicant’s lawyers and granted an extension. The application may proceed and will be programmed for conference.

Key holding: Where a short delay is caused by the applicant’s representative’s miscalculation rather than the applicant’s conduct, that representative error weighs in favour of an extension of time under s 366(2)(a).

This is representative error. The reason for the delay weights in favour of an extension of time.

entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: Jason Perry v Australian Port Service (Qld) Pty Ltd Trading AS Ausport Marine [2026] FWC 4146
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission resolved a s.739 dispute concerning the Ausport Marine enterprise agreement, principally the date for the first CPI wage increase and travel-time/reimbursement entitlements under cl 12(a). The Deputy President issued a recommendation answering five questions and confirmed that s.739 cannot be used to terminate the Agreement or revisit the BOOT.

Key holding: Clause 12(a) entitles an employee to reimbursement for kilometres and tolls only where the employer requires the employee to use their own vehicle, not where the employee chooses to do so.

Therefore, in my view, the entitlement to be reimbursed for distance travelled and tolls is limited to circumstances where the use of the employee's own vehicle is a requirement by the employer, not a choice by the employee.

entry.title: Doran Herrick v Bupa Aged Care Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4141
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4141, Mr Herrick lodged an unfair dismissal application after his May 2025 dismissal from Bupa Aged Care Australia Pty Ltd, despite having signed an Employee Separation Agreement containing release and bar-to-proceedings clauses. The Fair Work Commission found the agreement constituted a binding settlement, declined a stay, and dismissed the application under s 587(1)(c).

Key holding: A binding settlement or accord and satisfaction extinguishes the existing cause of action and replaces it with a new cause based on the agreement, so an unfair dismissal application barred by an executed separation agreement has no reasonable prospects of success.

In Australian Postal Corporation v Gorman1, Besanko J held that the existence of a binding settlement or 'accord and satisfaction' extinguishes the existing cause of action and replaces it with a new cause of action based on the agreement. That is the case in the matter before me.

entry.title: Charles Patterson v P.A.P. Heating Solutions Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4135
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission considered an unfair dismissal application by Mr Patterson against a small business employer, PAP Heating. The dismissal was for alleged performance issues, but the employer’s written warning did not state that dismissal was at risk and the employer terminated before a promised meeting. The Commission found the dismissal unfair and awarded compensation.

Key holding: To satisfy the “Other dismissal” limb of the Small Business Fair Dismissal Code, a small business employer must expressly warn the employee that dismissal is at risk if performance does not improve, not merely that further action may follow.

However, the warning did not say that Mr Pa tterson was at risk of being dismissed if there was no improvement. As a result, the dismissal was not consistent with the Small Business Code.

entry.title: Thomas McGuire v Woolworths Group Limited [2026] FWC 4140
entry.content:
Thomas McGuire was dismissed by Woolworths Group Limited on 8 August 2026 and filed an unfair dismissal application on 8 September 2026, outside the 21-day period. He sought an extension of time under s 394(2) of the Fair Work Act 2009. The Fair Work Commission refused the extension because it was not satisfied that exceptional circumstances existed under s 394(3).

Key holding: Mere ignorance of the Commission’s unfair dismissal jurisdiction or the 21-day time limit is not a sufficient basis for granting an extension of time under s 394(3).

Mere ignorance of the law is not a sufficient basis for the grant of additional time.

entry.title: Mr Adrian Clay v Peninsula Directional Drilling Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4077
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4077, the Fair Work Commission considered a jurisdictional objection to Mr Adrian Clay’s unfair dismissal application against Peninsula Directional Drilling Pty Ltd. Mr Clay was General Manager with guaranteed annual earnings of $235,000, above the high-income threshold, and the Commission found he was not covered by the Clerks—Private Sector Award 2020 because his principal purpose was managing the business, not clerical work. The unfair dismissal application was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

Key holding: Coverage under the Clerks—Private Sector Award 2020 requires the employee to be wholly or principally engaged in clerical work; incidental clerical duties do not establish coverage where the principal purpose of the role is management.

Having regard to the evidence of the duties and responsibilities of the work performed by Mr Clay, the extent to which he engaged in any clerical work as defined in the Award, was incidental. While I accept that some of the work performed by Mr Clay was clerical in nature, I am satisfied that he was not wholly or principally engaged in clerical work.

entry.title: Kawicki v Trustees of the Marist Brothers t/as Marist Brothers Sydney Province [2026] NSWCA 220
entry.content:
The appellant, a former student, sued the Trustees of the Marist Brothers for damages arising from sexual abuse by Brother Florentine; the primary judge awarded $186,000 but declined damages for diminished earning capacity. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal against the refusal of past economic loss, with Adamson JA dissenting. The appeal concerned only economic loss; liability for the sexual abuse and the $186,000 award were not in issue.

Key holding: A claimant alleging past economic loss from historical abuse bears the onus of proving that the abuse caused a diminution in earning capacity productive of actual financial loss; a tribunal may reject the claim by not being satisfied, without making a positive finding of no diminution.

A failure to be satisfied that there was a diminution in earning capacity is different from a finding that there was no diminution in earning capacity. The onus to establish a diminution in earning capacity rested on Mr Kawicki.

entry.content:

entry.title: Mr Johnathon Burr v The Trustee for Cornerstone Labour Hire Unit Trust [2026] FWC 4121
entry.content:
Mr Burr’s host assignment with CEVA Logistics ended and he brought an unfair dismissal application against his labour-hire employer, Cornerstone. The Commission had to decide whether Cornerstone dismissed him or whether only his host placement ended; because Cornerstone kept him on its books and sought alternative work, the application was dismissed.

Key holding: Where a labour-hire employee’s host placement ends but the labour-hire employer remains ready and actively attempts to redeploy the employee, the employment has not been terminated on the employer’s initiative and there is no dismissal under s 386(1).

Under s 386(1), a person is considered dismissed if their employment with the employer has been terminated on the employer's initiative. It follows that if the employment continues or if the employer is actively seeking to find alternative work for the employee, there has been no dismissal.

entry.title: Madana Harrop v Maryborough District Health Service [2026] FWC 4112
entry.content:
Ms Harrop lodged an unfair dismissal application 16 days late after her union, the ANMF, failed to transmit a legal referral due to an automated email system error. The Fair Work Commission accepted representative error as a reasonable explanation, found exceptional circumstances and granted an extension of time. The merits of the unfair dismissal claim have not yet been determined.

Key holding: Where an applicant is blameless and reasonably relies on their representative, a delay caused by the representative’s administrative or system error can be an acceptable explanation for the whole delay and support a finding of exceptional circumstances under s 394(3).

In this case, the reason for the delay was the error of the ANMF, and it is in my view reasonable for the Applicant to have relied on the ANMF's advice that referral would have been made to her legal representatives to pursue an unfair dismissal application. The Applicant should not be disadvantaged because the ANMF experienced a system error in processing of the legal referral.

entry.title: Stephanie Tranquille v New Beginnings Network [2026] FWC 4113
entry.content:
This was an application by New Beginnings Network to vary an unfair dismissal compensation order so that it could pay $5,025 by instalments of $50 per week, citing financial hardship. The Fair Work Commission refused the amount sought but varied the order to allow 10 weekly instalments of $502.50, with superannuation payable on the original due date.

Key holding: Under s 393 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission has a broad discretion to permit unfair dismissal compensation to be paid by instalments, exercised by weighing the respondent’s business needs and likely compliance against the applicant’s need to access compensation within a reasonable period.

In McCarron, James v Commercial Facilities Management Pty Ltd T/A CFM Air Conditioning Pty Ltd [2013] FWC 3577 in ordering that compensation be paid in instalments Bissett C said that when considering the time period for the instalment payments to be made the business needs of the Respondent must be weighed against the needs of the Applicant to access the compensation.
